title: Do education programmes for children and young people with disabilities in low- and middle-income countries work?

blocks.html: The question is: “In low- and middle-income countries, do programmes meant to improve education for children and young people with disabilities work, and which kinds work best?”

sentences: A Campbell systematic review found that a range of individual-level interventions work to improve educational outcomes among people with disabilities in low- and middle-income countries, but there is little research on systemic or school-level change [1].

The review authors call this evidence 'emerging support' for these interventions, and they say more research is needed to understand which types of interventions are most efficacious and how best to deliver them [1].
They also judge the quality of the included studies to be largely low [1].
So the sources support a qualified yes: some programmes, mostly those that build individual skills, show effects, but the sources cannot yet say firmly which kinds work best.
People with disabilities often fall behind their peers without disabilities in enrolment, retention and completion of education [1].
Evidence suggests that the gap in educational attainment between people with and without disabilities is greatest in low- and middle-income countries [1].
Before the review, its protocol noted that evidence on which interventions are effective in meeting international goals for disability and education had not been established [7].
The protocol also noted that past evidence syntheses had found very little literature examining educational outcomes that compared disabled and nondisabled peers in these countries [7].
According to the source, all but one study received an overall rating of low confidence in study findings [1].

According to the source, a twin-track approach is needed, which both addresses the specific needs of children with disabilities but also ensures that they are included in mainstream activities (e.g., through improving the skills of teachers and accessibility of the classroom) [1].

However, currently most interventions included in this systematic review targeted individual children with disabilities in an attempt to improve their functioning, skills, and competencies, but did not focus on mainstreaming these children into the school by system-level or school-level changes [1].

According to the source (Hunt, Saran, White & Kuper, March 2025), "consequently, a focus on evaluation of interventions which target not just the individual with a disability but also their broader environment [is/are] needed" [1].

The source, a systematic review titled "Effectiveness of interventions for improving educational outcomes for people with disabilities in low‐ and middle‐income countries: A systematic review," is supplied here only as a title with no findings or certainty language, so no conclusion about effectiveness can be attributed to it [1].

blocks.text: Interventions that build skills for learning

sentences: Of the 18 studies included in the review's analysis of intervention effects on 'Skills for learning', 12 interventions had a significant effect [1].
The review reports significant effects on literacy, cognitive skills, handwriting and numeracy [1].
The authors note that all these effects are large but are based on a low number of studies [1].

blocks.text: Conditions for inclusion and teacher-focused interventions

sentences: Studies concerned with 'Conditions for inclusion of people with disabilities in education' showed a moderately significant effect [1].
One study concerned with teacher knowledge showed a significant effect size [1].

Only one study achieved the aim of improving attendance, enrolment and completion by equipping mainstream settings for children with disabilities, and it did so by improving teacher knowledge and attitudes about inclusive education [1].

blocks.text: Gaps and weaknesses in the evidence

sentences: Most interventions tried to improve children's skills but did not focus on system-level or school-level changes [1].
The included studies all used different interventions and outcome measures, which makes direct comparison difficult [1].
None of the studies were undertaken in humanitarian settings, and few disaggregated their findings by gender [1].
Most study designs could not account for many potential confounders, and masking, baseline balance and attribution were poorly reported [1].
The review concludes that more systemic approaches are needed to improve access to education and the likelihood of successful engagement in it [1].

blocks.text: Programme examples and guidance from a UNESCO guide

sentences: A UNESCO guide on inclusion and equity includes examples of initiatives that it describes as contributing to more inclusive and equitable education systems [6].

In one example from Ethiopia, Handicap International piloted an approach in which six 'cluster schools', enrolling over 700 students, became inclusive and supported 30 satellite schools in applying similar practices [6].

The guide reports that this led to improvements in inclusive education practice, better physical accessibility, increased enrolment for children with disabilities and a better learning environment for all students [6].
In Cambodia, the guide reports, it quickly became obvious that an itinerant teacher system for children with disabilities should also focus on the quality of education for all children [6].

The guide cites strong evidence of the potential of approaches that encourage cooperation between students, and says this evidence suggests such practices can be effective in supporting learners with disabilities, although orchestrating them requires skill [6].
The guide does not tie this cooperative-learning evidence specifically to low- and middle-income countries [6].
The guide also warns that inclusion efforts that depend on practices imported from special education tend to foster new and more subtle forms of segregation within mainstream settings [6].
The studies concerned with speech and school behaviour showed no significant effect of intervention [1].
Across the studies, heterogeneity is high, and the risk of publication bias varies but was frequently high [1].
All but one of the studies reviewed were rated low confidence in their findings overall [1].
Low confidence in the evidence across studies was largely due to the use of low-rigour study designs, and did not always reflect multiple points of weakness within any single study [1].

A twin-track approach is needed, one that addresses children with disabilities' specific needs while also including them in mainstream activities, for example by improving teachers' skills and classroom accessibility [1].

A systematic review found that most evaluated interventions targeted individual children with disabilities to improve their functioning, skills and competencies, rather than mainstreaming them through school-level or system-level changes [1].
The authors conclude that evaluation is needed of interventions that target not only the individual with a disability but also their broader environment [1].

The best-supported claim is that a range of individual-level interventions, mostly aimed at building children's skills, can improve educational outcomes for people with disabilities in low- and middle-income countries.
The strongest results are for skills for learning, but those large effects rest on few studies of largely low quality.
Evidence on school-level and system-level approaches, including teacher training, is thin, and the main finding on teachers comes from a single study.
The review set out to ask which interventions appear most effective for different types of disability, but these passages do not report an answer to that question [1].
On which kinds work best, the review's own conclusion is that more research is needed [1].

Findings in our sources we judged outside this question

Judged not material to this question: “Twenty‐eight studies were included in this review.” (Effectiveness of interventions for improving educational outcomes for people wit [1]).

Judged not material to this question: “Most studies ( n = 25) targeted children with disabilities.” (Effectiveness of interventions for improving educational outcomes for people wit [1]).

Judged not material to this question: “Only two studies directly targeted family members, and the remaining three focused on service providers.” (Effectiveness of interventions for improving educational outcomes for people wit [1]).

Judged not material to this question: “Individuals with intellectual or learning and developmental impairments were most frequently targeted by interventions ( n = 17).” (Effectiveness of interventions for improving educational outcomes for people wit [1]).

Judged not material to this question: “The category of interventions most represented across studies was ‘Educational attainment support’, for instance, a reading comprehension intervention that combined strategy instruction (graphic organisers, visual …” (Effectiveness of interventions for improving educational outcomes for people wit [1]).

Outside this question: “Children with disabilities fall behind in educational outcomes as the current school systems are not set up to teach children with different impairment types.” (Effectiveness of interventions for improving educational outcomes for people wit [1]).

Outside this question: “There is no one ‘magic bullet’ intervention which can equalise health outcomes for this group.” (Effectiveness of interventions for improving educational outcomes for people wit [1]).
